title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 3.2.1 Reading: Intensive Reading (Comprehension)

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Intensive reading means reading a text closely enough to understand both what it says and what it suggests. In this sub-strand you will read a passage of about 300 words on etiquette, answer factual and inferential questions, and practise skimming and scanning so you can find information quickly.

## Strand 3.0: Etiquette
Sub-strand 3.2.1: Reading: Intensive Reading (Comprehension)
Suggested lessons: 3

## What this sub-strand covers
• Text (300 words)
• Factual information
• Inferential information

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Language Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 3.0 Etiquette, Sub-strand 3.2.1 Intensive Reading: Comprehension

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) read a text of about 300 words for comprehension
b) apply appropriate reading skills to obtain both factual and inferential information from a text
c) recommend intensive reading in their day-to- day life

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why do we read?
2. How can we read faster?

PAGE 2: How we will learn

## Learning experiences
• read a variety of print and non-print texts of about 300 words
• identify events in a story or a passage of about 300 words with logical and fluent flow
• answer factual and inferential questions from a text of about 300 words
• work together to infer the meaning of vocabulary from contexts
• skim through a digital text of about 300 words focusing mainly on the title and illustrations
• scan for information such as vocabulary words and answer questions from print or digital text
• skim or scan a comic, magazine, newspaper or age-appropriate reader
• discuss and role-play events in texts based on the theme

## Core competencies
• Critical thinking and problem solving: This is developed as the learner uses logical thinking to answer factual and inferential questions from a text of about 300 words.
• Digital Literacy: It is promoted as the learner is able to interact with digital devices to skim through digital texts focusing on the title and illustrations.

## Values
• Social Justice: This is promoted as the learner accords peers equal opportunities to infer the meaning of vocabulary from contexts.
• Respect: This is developed as the learner is able to demonstrate etiquette when dealing with peers in class during common tasks.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Citizenship: This is fostered as the learner works with peers peacefully during group activities.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to connect the concept of etiquette and politeness to their daily interactions and in all other learning areas.

PAGE 3: Lesson 1: Reading a longer passage

LESSON 1: READING A LONGER PASSAGE
==================================

## What you will learn
• Read a passage of about 300 words from beginning to end.
• List the events in the order they happen.
• Retell the passage in a few clear sentences.

Curriculum outcomes: a) read a text of about 300 words for comprehension

## Introduction
A short sign is easy to remember. A passage of about 300 words asks for more. You follow several events, several speakers, and a lesson at the end. The way through is to read steadily and keep the order.

## Notes

### How to read a longer text
Do not race, and do not stop at every word. Read a paragraph, picture it, then move on. If a sentence is hard, finish the paragraph and come back. The later sentences often explain the earlier ones.

Keep three questions in mind: Who is here? What happens next? What changes by the end?

PAGE 4: Lesson 1: Reading a longer passage — The Polite Visitor

### The Polite Visitor
Last Saturday, Neema was sweeping the compound when someone knocked at the gate. She put the broom down and walked over. A man she had never seen stood outside. He carried a small brown bag and a folded letter.

Neema remembered her mother's words. A child should greet people kindly, but a child should not open the gate for a stranger when no adult is near. She stayed inside the compound, smiled, and said, "Good morning, sir. Please wait a moment. I will call my mother."

Her mother came quickly, wiping her hands on a cloth. "Welcome," she said. "May I help you?"

PAGE 5: Lesson 1: Reading a longer passage — Notes 3

The man took off his hat. "Excuse me, madam. I beg your pardon for coming without notice. Your brother sent me with this letter. He asked me to bring it today."

Mother opened the gate then. "Thank you for making the long walk," she said. "Please come and sit on the bench." She turned to Neema. "Please bring our visitor a cup of water."

Neema brought the water with both hands. "Here you are, sir."

"Thank you," said the man. "You have good manners. Please tell your uncle that the letter is about a family meeting next month. I am sorry I cannot stay for tea. I must reach the next home before the sun is high."

PAGE 6: Lesson 1: Reading a longer passage — Notes 4

Mother walked with him to the road. "Thank you again. Travel safely."

When they were alone, Mother held Neema's hand. "You did well," she said. "You were polite, and you were also careful. Good manners are not only pretty words. They show respect, and they help us live safely with other people. The next time a visitor comes, use the same courtesy."

Neema nodded. She wanted to remember every polite phrase she had heard that morning: good morning, please, welcome, may I, excuse me, I beg your pardon, thank you, and I am sorry. She wrote them in her exercise book so she could use them again.

### The events in order
1. Neema is sweeping when a stranger knocks.
2. She greets him but does not open the gate. She calls her mother.
3. Mother welcomes the man, who has brought a letter from Neema's uncle.
4. Neema brings water. The man explains the letter and leaves.
5. Mother praises Neema for being both polite and careful.
6. Neema writes the polite phrases in her book.

PAGE 7: Lesson 1: Reading a longer passage — Retell it

### Retell it
A retelling is short and uses your own sentences. Neema met a stranger at the gate, called her mother, and served water after the man was welcomed. The letter was about a family meeting. Neema learnt that good manners include both kind words and care.

That retelling leaves out the hat and the cloth, and that is fine. It keeps the people, the order and the lesson.

## Key words
• passage — a piece of writing that is read as one text
• compound — the open ground around a home, inside the fence or gate
• retell — to tell a text again in your own words, keeping the important events

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Why did Neema stay inside the gate at first?

Working:
1. Find the paragraph where she remembers her mother's words.
2. She was told not to open the gate to a stranger when no adult was near.

Answer: A child should not open the gate to a stranger when no adult is near.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
What was the letter about?

Working:
1. Look near the end of the man's visit.
2. He asks Neema to tell her uncle about a family meeting.

Answer: A family meeting next month.

PAGE 8: Lesson 1: Reading a longer passage — Answers to practice

## Activity: Read and order the events
You will need: The passage The Polite Visitor, Strips of paper or an exercise book

1. Read the passage silently from start to finish.

2. Read it again in pairs, taking turns at each paragraph.

3. Write the six events in order without looking, then check them against the text.

4. Each learner retells the passage to a partner in four or five sentences.

## Practice

1. What was Neema doing when she heard the knock?

2. Who sent the letter?

3. What did Neema bring the visitor?

4. What did Neema do with the polite phrases after the visitor left?

## Answers to practice

1. She was sweeping the compound.

2. Neema's uncle (her mother's brother).

3. A cup of water.

4. She wrote them in her exercise book.

## Summary
• Read a longer passage steadily, paragraph by paragraph.
• Keep the events in order.
• A retelling uses your own sentences and keeps the important facts.

PAGE 9: Lesson 2: Factual and inferential questions — Factual information

LESSON 2: FACTUAL AND INFERENTIAL QUESTIONS
===========================================

## What you will learn
• Answer factual questions by pointing to the text.
• Answer inferential questions by using clues.
• Work out the meaning of a word from the sentences around it.

Curriculum outcomes: b) apply appropriate reading skills to obtain both factual and inferential information from a text

## Introduction
Some questions point at a sentence and wait for you to find it. Others point at a gap and wait for you to think. Both kinds belong to intensive reading, and they are not the same skill.

## Notes

### Factual information
A factual question asks for a fact the writer states. You can put your finger on the words. From The Polite Visitor:

- What did the man carry? A small brown bag and a folded letter.
- What did Mother ask Neema to bring? A cup of water.
- Why did the man refuse tea? He had to reach the next home before the sun was high.

If you cannot point to the place, you may be guessing. Go back to the passage.

### Inferential information
An inference is a careful conclusion from clues. The writer does not say it in one ready sentence.

PAGE 10: Lesson 2: Factual and inferential questions — Notes 3

- Why did Neema bring the water with both hands? The passage says she has good manners. Using both hands is a respectful way to offer a drink. The text does not say "both hands means respect", but her mother's lesson and the man's praise support that reading.
- How did Mother feel at the end? She held Neema's hand and said "You did well." Those actions suggest she was pleased and proud.
- Was the man in a hurry? He apologised for not staying for tea and said he must reach the next home before the sun was high. Yes, he was in a hurry.

PAGE 11: Lesson 2: Factual and inferential questions — Vocabulary from context

A good inference uses clues. "I think the man was a king" uses no clue from this passage, so it is not a fair inference.

### Vocabulary from context
Context means the words around a new word.

- Courtesy, in Mother's last speech, sits next to polite, respect and living safely with other people. Courtesy means polite behaviour.
- Without notice means the man had not sent word that he was coming. We know this because he apologises for arriving that way, and the family did not expect him.
- Compound is the place Neema was sweeping, inside the gate. It is the open ground around the home.

Say the meaning in your own words, then check that your meaning still fits the sentence.

### Share the thinking
When a group infers, each person should get a turn to name a clue. Listening to another clue may improve your answer. You can disagree and still be polite: "I see that clue, and I also noticed this sentence."

## Key words
• factual — stated directly in the text so you can point to it
• inferential — understood from clues rather than from one direct sentence
• context — the words and sentences around a word that help to show its meaning
• inference — a conclusion you draw from clues

PAGE 12: Lesson 2: Factual and inferential questions — Example 1

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Is this question factual or inferential? "What did the man carry?"

Working:
1. The first paragraph states the objects.
2. You can point to the sentence.

Answer: Factual. He carried a small brown bag and a folded letter.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
What does courtesy mean in the passage? Use the context.

Working:
1. Mother connects good manners, respect and living safely with other people.
2. She then says to use the same courtesy.

Answer: Polite, respectful behaviour.

## Activity: Facts, inferences and new words
You will need: The passage The Polite Visitor, Two columns in an exercise book labelled Fact and Inference

1. Answer three factual questions by reading the matching sentence aloud.

2. Answer two inferential questions. Each person names the clue they used.

3. Work together on the words courtesy, notice and compound. Agree a meaning from the context.

4. Give every learner a turn to speak. Thank a partner who adds a clue you had missed.

PAGE 13: Lesson 2: Factual and inferential questions — Answers to practice

## Practice

1. Give one factual detail about how the man greeted Mother.

2. Why can we infer that Mother was pleased with Neema?

3. What does "without notice" mean in the man's apology?

4. Why is "The man was a king" not a fair inference?

## Answers to practice

1. He said, "Excuse me, madam. I beg your pardon for coming without notice."

2. She held Neema's hand and said, "You did well."

3. He came without telling the family beforehand.

4. The passage gives no clue that he was a king. An inference must come from the text.

## Summary
• Factual answers are written in the passage.
• Inferential answers join clues.
• The sentences around a word help you say what it means.

PAGE 14: Lesson 3: Skimming, scanning and reading often

LESSON 3: SKIMMING, SCANNING AND READING OFTEN
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Skim a text using the title and the opening lines.
• Scan a text for a particular word or fact.
• Give reasons for reading carefully in everyday life.

Curriculum outcomes: b) apply appropriate reading skills to obtain both factual and inferential information from a text; c) recommend intensive reading in their day-to- day life

## Introduction
You do not always need every word on a first look. Sometimes you need the topic in a few seconds. Sometimes you need one name in a crowd of sentences. Skimming and scanning are the fast tools. Intensive reading is the careful one you use next.

PAGE 15: Lesson 3: Skimming, scanning and reading often — Scanning

## Notes

### Skimming
To skim is to move quickly over a text for the general idea. You use:

- the title
- pictures or headings
- the first sentence of the piece
- a glance at names that repeat

You do not read every line. After a skim of The Polite Visitor you should be able to say: it is about a girl, a stranger at the gate, and polite behaviour. You would not yet know the colour of the bag.

### Scanning
To scan is to look for a particular item: a word, a name, a time or a phrase. Let your eyes hunt. When you find "family meeting", stop and read that sentence properly.

Scan The Polite Visitor for these and say the sentence you land on:

- the word bench
- the phrase good manners
- the name of the month's event (a family meeting)

Scanning is how you find vocabulary your teacher has listed, or an answer you remember seeing.

PAGE 16: Lesson 3: Skimming, scanning and reading often — A second short text to practise on

### A second short text to practise on
Classroom Courtesy

Our class wrote three rules and pinned them beside the door. The first rule says, "Say excuse me before you interrupt." The second says, "Ask with may I and please." The third says, "Thank the person who helps you."

On Monday, Peter wanted the chalkboard ruler. He waited until the teacher finished her sentence. Then he said, "Excuse me, may I borrow the ruler, please?" She smiled and passed it to him. When he returned it he said, "Thank you."

The rules are short, but they changed the noise in the room. Learners spent less time arguing and more time listening.

Skim: the title and the first sentence tell you the text is about class rules on courtesy.
Scan: find the three rules, or find what Peter borrowed (the chalkboard ruler).

PAGE 17: Lesson 3: Skimming, scanning and reading often — Why keep doing this

### Then read intensively
Fast tools do not replace careful reading. Skim to choose a text, scan to find a place, then read that part closely for factual and inferential questions.

### Why keep doing this
Every day you meet notes from teachers, stories, instructions on packets, and messages at home. Careful reading stops you missing a time, a warning or a kind request. It also grows your vocabulary, so the next page is easier.

Recommend it to someone else. Tell a brother or a sister: look at the title first, hunt for the fact you need, then read that part properly. Intensive reading is not only a school exercise. It is how you understand the texts that fill ordinary days.

You can practise on a comic, a children's page of a magazine, or a reader your teacher lends you. Role-play a scene after you read it. If you can act what happened, you have understood it.

PAGE 18: Lesson 3: Skimming, scanning and reading often — Example 1

## Key words
• skim — to look quickly at a text for the general idea
• scan — to look quickly through a text for a particular fact or word
• rule — a guide for what people should do

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You need only the topic of Classroom Courtesy. Do you skim or scan?

Working:
1. The topic is the general idea.
2. Skimming uses the title and the opening.
3. Scanning is for one detail.

Answer: Skim. The title and first sentence show it is about class rules on courtesy.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Find what Peter borrowed. Which skill do you use?

Working:
1. You want one object.
2. Move your eyes until you see borrow.
3. Read that sentence.

Answer: Scan. He borrowed the chalkboard ruler.

PAGE 19: Lesson 3: Skimming, scanning and reading often — Skim, scan, then act

## Activity: Skim, scan, then act
You will need: The Polite Visitor, Classroom Courtesy, A comic, magazine or reader if one is in the classroom

1. Skim Classroom Courtesy using only the title and the first sentence. Say the topic in one line.

2. Scan both texts for the words please, thank you and excuse me. Count how many times you find each.

3. If a comic, magazine or reader is available, skim the title and pictures, then scan for one interesting word.

4. Role-play Peter's request or Neema's greeting. Speak the polite words clearly.

## Practice

1. What is the difference between skimming and scanning?

2. Scan Classroom Courtesy: what are the three rules about?

3. After you skim and scan, what should you still do with an important paragraph?

4. Give one reason to recommend intensive reading to someone at home.

PAGE 20: Lesson 3: Skimming, scanning and reading often — Answers to practice

## Answers to practice

1. Skimming looks for the general idea. Scanning looks for a particular word or fact.

2. Say excuse me before you interrupt; ask with may I and please; thank the person who helps you.

3. Read it carefully so you can answer factual and inferential questions.

4. It helps them understand notes, stories and instructions, and it builds vocabulary for the next text.

## Summary
• Skim for the topic. Scan for a detail. Then read important parts carefully.
• Context and clues still do the deeper work.
• Careful reading is useful every day, not only in an English lesson.

PAGE 21: Revision quiz

REVISION QUIZ
=============

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. What was Neema doing at the start of The Polite Visitor?
   A. Reading a letter
   B. Sweeping the compound
   C. Cooking tea
   D. Opening the gate

2. Why did Neema not open the gate at once?
   A. The gate was locked and she had no key
   B. She had been taught not to open it to a stranger when no adult was near
   C. She did not hear the knock
   D. Mother told her to hide

3. What did the visitor bring?
   A. A cake and a ribbon
   B. A small brown bag and a letter
   C. A cup of water
   D. A school form

4. The letter was about ____.
   A. a football match
   B. a family meeting next month
   C. a lost pencil
   D. a new gate

5. Which question is inferential?
   A. What did Neema bring the man?
   B. What colour was the bag?
   C. How did Mother feel about Neema's actions?
   D. What was Neema sweeping with?

6. What does courtesy mean in Mother's speech?

7. Which skill gives you the general idea of a text quickly?
   A. Scanning for one word
   B. Skimming the title and opening
   C. Copying every paragraph
   D. Skipping the title

8. You want to find the word bench in the passage. What do you do?

9. In Classroom Courtesy, what did Peter borrow?
   A. A cup
   B. The chalkboard ruler
   C. A letter
   D. A hat

10. Why is intensive reading useful outside the English lesson?

PAGE 22: Quiz answers

ANSWERS
=======

1. B. Sweeping the compound
   The first sentence says she was sweeping the compound.

2. B. She had been taught not to open it to a stranger when no adult was near
   She remembered her mother's words and called her instead.

3. B. A small brown bag and a letter
   The first paragraph states these two objects.

4. B. a family meeting next month
   The man asks Neema to tell her uncle that.

5. C. How did Mother feel about Neema's actions?
   Feelings are shown by clues, such as holding Neema's hand and saying she did well. The other answers are stated directly.

6. Polite, respectful behaviour.
   The nearby sentences talk about good manners, respect and living safely with others.

7. B. Skimming the title and opening
   Skimming uses the title, pictures and opening for the topic.

8. Scan the passage until your eyes find bench, then read that sentence.
   Scanning hunts for a particular word.

9. B. The chalkboard ruler
   He asked to borrow the chalkboard ruler.

10. It helps you understand everyday texts such as notes, stories and instructions, and it builds vocabulary.
   Careful reading is a daily skill.

2. She was told not to open the gate to a stranger when no adult was near.

Answer: A child should not open the gate to a stranger when no adult is near.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
What was the letter about?

Working:
1. Look near the end of the man's visit.
2. He asks Neema to tell her uncle about a family meeting.

Answer: A family meeting next month.

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Reading a longer passage — Answers to practice
studyPages.body:
## Activity: Read and order the events
You will need: The passage The Polite Visitor, Strips of paper or an exercise book

1. Read the passage silently from start to finish.

2. Read it again in pairs, taking turns at each paragraph.

3. Write the six events in order without looking, then check them against the text.

4. Each learner retells the passage to a partner in four or five sentences.

## Practice

1. What was Neema doing when she heard the knock?

2. Who sent the letter?

3. What did Neema bring the visitor?

4. What did Neema do with the polite phrases after the visitor left?

## Answers to practice

1. She was sweeping the compound.

2. Neema's uncle (her mother's brother).

3. A cup of water.

4. She wrote them in her exercise book.

## Summary
• Read a longer passage steadily, paragraph by paragraph.
• Keep the events in order.
• A retelling uses your own sentences and keeps the important facts.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Factual and inferential questions — Factual information
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: FACTUAL AND INFERENTIAL QUESTIONS
===========================================

## What you will learn
• Answer factual questions by pointing to the text.
• Answer inferential questions by using clues.
• Work out the meaning of a word from the sentences around it.

Curriculum outcomes: b) apply appropriate reading skills to obtain both factual and inferential information from a text

## Introduction
Some questions point at a sentence and wait for you to find it. Others point at a gap and wait for you to think. Both kinds belong to intensive reading, and they are not the same skill.

## Notes

### Factual information
A factual question asks for a fact the writer states. You can put your finger on the words. From The Polite Visitor:

- What did the man carry? A small brown bag and a folded letter.
- What did Mother ask Neema to bring? A cup of water.
- Why did the man refuse tea? He had to reach the next home before the sun was high.

If you cannot point to the place, you may be guessing. Go back to the passage.

### Inferential information
An inference is a careful conclusion from clues. The writer does not say it in one ready sentence.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Factual and inferential questions — Notes 3
studyPages.body:
- Why did Neema bring the water with both hands? The passage says she has good manners. Using both hands is a respectful way to offer a drink. The text does not say "both hands means respect", but her mother's lesson and the man's praise support that reading.
- How did Mother feel at the end? She held Neema's hand and said "You did well." Those actions suggest she was pleased and proud.
- Was the man in a hurry? He apologised for not staying for tea and said he must reach the next home before the sun was high. Yes, he was in a hurry.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Factual and inferential questions — Vocabulary from context
studyPages.body:
A good inference uses clues. "I think the man was a king" uses no clue from this passage, so it is not a fair inference.

### Vocabulary from context
Context means the words around a new word.

- Courtesy, in Mother's last speech, sits next to polite, respect and living safely with other people. Courtesy means polite behaviour.
- Without notice means the man had not sent word that he was coming. We know this because he apologises for arriving that way, and the family did not expect him.
- Compound is the place Neema was sweeping, inside the gate. It is the open ground around the home.

Say the meaning in your own words, then check that your meaning still fits the sentence.

### Share the thinking
When a group infers, each person should get a turn to name a clue. Listening to another clue may improve your answer. You can disagree and still be polite: "I see that clue, and I also noticed this sentence."

## Key words
• factual — stated directly in the text so you can point to it
• inferential — understood from clues rather than from one direct sentence
• context — the words and sentences around a word that help to show its meaning
• inference — a conclusion you draw from clues

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Factual and inferential questions — Example 1
studyPages.body:
## Worked examples

### Example 1
Is this question factual or inferential? "What did the man carry?"

Working:
1. The first paragraph states the objects.
2. You can point to the sentence.

Answer: Factual. He carried a small brown bag and a folded letter.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
What does courtesy mean in the passage? Use the context.

Working:
1. Mother connects good manners, respect and living safely with other people.
2. She then says to use the same courtesy.

Answer: Polite, respectful behaviour.

## Activity: Facts, inferences and new words
You will need: The passage The Polite Visitor, Two columns in an exercise book labelled Fact and Inference

1. Answer three factual questions by reading the matching sentence aloud.

2. Answer two inferential questions. Each person names the clue they used.

3. Work together on the words courtesy, notice and compound. Agree a meaning from the context.

4. Give every learner a turn to speak. Thank a partner who adds a clue you had missed.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Factual and inferential questions — Answers to practice
studyPages.body:
## Practice

1. Give one factual detail about how the man greeted Mother.

2. Why can we infer that Mother was pleased with Neema?

3. What does "without notice" mean in the man's apology?

4. Why is "The man was a king" not a fair inference?

## Answers to practice

1. He said, "Excuse me, madam. I beg your pardon for coming without notice."

2. She held Neema's hand and said, "You did well."

3. He came without telling the family beforehand.

4. The passage gives no clue that he was a king. An inference must come from the text.

## Summary
• Factual answers are written in the passage.
• Inferential answers join clues.
• The sentences around a word help you say what it means.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Skimming, scanning and reading often
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: SKIMMING, SCANNING AND READING OFTEN
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Skim a text using the title and the opening lines.
• Scan a text for a particular word or fact.
• Give reasons for reading carefully in everyday life.

Curriculum outcomes: b) apply appropriate reading skills to obtain both factual and inferential information from a text; c) recommend intensive reading in their day-to- day life

## Introduction
You do not always need every word on a first look. Sometimes you need the topic in a few seconds. Sometimes you need one name in a crowd of sentences. Skimming and scanning are the fast tools. Intensive reading is the careful one you use next.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Skimming, scanning and reading often — Scanning
studyPages.body:
## Notes

### Skimming
To skim is to move quickly over a text for the general idea. You use:

- the title
- pictures or headings
- the first sentence of the piece
- a glance at names that repeat

You do not read every line. After a skim of The Polite Visitor you should be able to say: it is about a girl, a stranger at the gate, and polite behaviour. You would not yet know the colour of the bag.

### Scanning
To scan is to look for a particular item: a word, a name, a time or a phrase. Let your eyes hunt. When you find "family meeting", stop and read that sentence properly.

Scan The Polite Visitor for these and say the sentence you land on:

- the word bench
- the phrase good manners
- the name of the month's event (a family meeting)

Scanning is how you find vocabulary your teacher has listed, or an answer you remember seeing.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Skimming, scanning and reading often — A second short text to practise on
studyPages.body:
### A second short text to practise on
Classroom Courtesy

Our class wrote three rules and pinned them beside the door. The first rule says, "Say excuse me before you interrupt." The second says, "Ask with may I and please." The third says, "Thank the person who helps you."

On Monday, Peter wanted the chalkboard ruler. He waited until the teacher finished her sentence. Then he said, "Excuse me, may I borrow the ruler, please?" She smiled and passed it to him. When he returned it he said, "Thank you."

The rules are short, but they changed the noise in the room. Learners spent less time arguing and more time listening.

Skim: the title and the first sentence tell you the text is about class rules on courtesy.
Scan: find the three rules, or find what Peter borrowed (the chalkboard ruler).

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Skimming, scanning and reading often — Why keep doing this
studyPages.body:
### Then read intensively
Fast tools do not replace careful reading. Skim to choose a text, scan to find a place, then read that part closely for factual and inferential questions.

### Why keep doing this
Every day you meet notes from teachers, stories, instructions on packets, and messages at home. Careful reading stops you missing a time, a warning or a kind request. It also grows your vocabulary, so the next page is easier.

Recommend it to someone else. Tell a brother or a sister: look at the title first, hunt for the fact you need, then read that part properly. Intensive reading is not only a school exercise. It is how you understand the texts that fill ordinary days.

You can practise on a comic, a children's page of a magazine, or a reader your teacher lends you. Role-play a scene after you read it. If you can act what happened, you have understood it.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Skimming, scanning and reading often — Example 1
studyPages.body:
## Key words
• skim — to look quickly at a text for the general idea
• scan — to look quickly through a text for a particular fact or word
• rule — a guide for what people should do

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You need only the topic of Classroom Courtesy. Do you skim or scan?

Working:
1. The topic is the general idea.
2. Skimming uses the title and the opening.
3. Scanning is for one detail.

Answer: Skim. The title and first sentence show it is about class rules on courtesy.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Find what Peter borrowed. Which skill do you use?

Working:
1. You want one object.
2. Move your eyes until you see borrow.
3. Read that sentence.

Answer: Scan. He borrowed the chalkboard ruler.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Skimming, scanning and reading often — Skim, scan, then act
studyPages.body:
## Activity: Skim, scan, then act
You will need: The Polite Visitor, Classroom Courtesy, A comic, magazine or reader if one is in the classroom

1. Skim Classroom Courtesy using only the title and the first sentence. Say the topic in one line.

2. Scan both texts for the words please, thank you and excuse me. Count how many times you find each.

3. If a comic, magazine or reader is available, skim the title and pictures, then scan for one interesting word.

4. Role-play Peter's request or Neema's greeting. Speak the polite words clearly.

## Practice

1. What is the difference between skimming and scanning?

2. Scan Classroom Courtesy: what are the three rules about?

3. After you skim and scan, what should you still do with an important paragraph?

4. Give one reason to recommend intensive reading to someone at home.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Skimming, scanning and reading often — Answers to practice
studyPages.body:
## Answers to practice

1. Skimming looks for the general idea. Scanning looks for a particular word or fact.

2. Say excuse me before you interrupt; ask with may I and please; thank the person who helps you.

3. Read it carefully so you can answer factual and inferential questions.

4. It helps them understand notes, stories and instructions, and it builds vocabulary for the next text.

## Summary
• Skim for the topic. Scan for a detail. Then read important parts carefully.
• Context and clues still do the deeper work.
• Careful reading is useful every day, not only in an English lesson.

studyPages.title: Revision quiz
studyPages.body:
REVISION QUIZ
=============

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. What was Neema doing at the start of The Polite Visitor?
   A. Reading a letter
   B. Sweeping the compound
   C. Cooking tea
   D. Opening the gate

2. Why did Neema not open the gate at once?
   A. The gate was locked and she had no key
   B. She had been taught not to open it to a stranger when no adult was near
   C. She did not hear the knock
   D. Mother told her to hide

3. What did the visitor bring?
   A. A cake and a ribbon
   B. A small brown bag and a letter
   C. A cup of water
   D. A school form

4. The letter was about ____.
   A. a football match
   B. a family meeting next month
   C. a lost pencil
   D. a new gate

5. Which question is inferential?
   A. What did Neema bring the man?
   B. What colour was the bag?
   C. How did Mother feel about Neema's actions?
   D. What was Neema sweeping with?

6. What does courtesy mean in Mother's speech?

7. Which skill gives you the general idea of a text quickly?
   A. Scanning for one word
   B. Skimming the title and opening
   C. Copying every paragraph
   D. Skipping the title

8. You want to find the word bench in the passage. What do you do?

9. In Classroom Courtesy, what did Peter borrow?
   A. A cup
   B. The chalkboard ruler
   C. A letter
   D. A hat

10. Why is intensive reading useful outside the English lesson?

studyPages.title: Quiz answers
studyPages.body:
ANSWERS
=======

1. B. Sweeping the compound
   The first sentence says she was sweeping the compound.

2. B. She had been taught not to open it to a stranger when no adult was near
   She remembered her mother's words and called her instead.

3. B. A small brown bag and a letter
   The first paragraph states these two objects.

4. B. a family meeting next month
   The man asks Neema to tell her uncle that.

5. C. How did Mother feel about Neema's actions?
   Feelings are shown by clues, such as holding Neema's hand and saying she did well. The other answers are stated directly.

6. Polite, respectful behaviour.
   The nearby sentences talk about good manners, respect and living safely with others.

7. B. Skimming the title and opening
   Skimming uses the title, pictures and opening for the topic.

8. Scan the passage until your eyes find bench, then read that sentence.
   Scanning hunts for a particular word.

9. B. The chalkboard ruler
   He asked to borrow the chalkboard ruler.

10. It helps you understand everyday texts such as notes, stories and instructions, and it builds vocabulary.
   Careful reading is a daily skill.
